title: Cross-Cutting
description: Cross-cutting alternates two or more locations or action lines, often implying they are happening at the same time. Each side of the join is a complete strand; the engine is meanwhile, two clocks racing.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: A baptism in one room. Killings in others.
The film does not wait for one to finish. It braids them so ritual and murder share a tense.

Or: a team at a door, a listener at another door, and the cut teaches you they are about to meet until a reverse proves they are not. Use it when simultaneity, comparison, or false geography is the engine.
It is the wrong tool when you need one compressed idea from unlike images: that is Montage. It is also the wrong tool when two rooms must be visible at once: that is Split Screen.
Fair misdirection relies on inference. Do not show matching house numbers and then pretend the doors were different.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Shoot each line so it can be interrupted: clear geography, readable time of day or clock, compatible but not identical details if you plan a wrong-door surprise. Alternate with tightening duration if you want the clocks to race.
Sound can bleed across (a bell, a vow) to bind the lines. Prompt: cross-cutting between [Subject] and a simultaneous other line, suspense by alternation, two clocks racing.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it for a raid versus a doorbell, a ritual versus a crime, dream levels that must tick together. Do not use it to dump unused coverage of one scene.
If there is no second clock, you are just cutting.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Montage collides images to make an argument or to compress months; cross-cutting keeps parallel actions alive. A Smash Cut is one contrast join, not a braid.
Split Screen shows both lines at once instead of alternating. An L-cut lets sound from one line sit on the picture of the other without changing the picture's location.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Godfather baptizes Michael while the rival killings land in other rooms. The Silence of the Lambs intercuts an FBI raid with a doorbell, then reveals the geography was wrong.
Inception alternates dream levels so one clock pressures another. Use the braid, not the blocking.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Cross-cutting between [Subject] and a simultaneous other line, suspense by alternation, two clocks racing. Name both geographies, what the viewer is invited to assume, and whether that assumption is true.
For video, two distinct spaces, alternating shots, tightening duration. Do not morph one room into the other.

Generate A: a team approaches a building and presses a doorbell. Generate B: someone in a similar interior hears a bell and walks toward a door. Intercut as though they connect. Reveal in a wide reverse that B opens to a lone courier at a different address. Keep the earlier shots ambiguous rather than contradictory.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Montage (idea by collision) or Split Screen (both at once). The tell: the second line has no clock, or both lines are clearly the same hallway.
The fix: two geographies, implied simultaneity, a reveal if you are lying about the door.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Cross-Cutting in film?
Cross-cutting alternates locations or action lines, usually to imply they are simultaneous. Each side of the join is its own strand; the cut says meanwhile.
Cross-Cutting vs Montage
Montage juxtaposes shots to compress time or produce an idea. Cross-cutting keeps two (or more) ongoing actions in play and braids them. One argues; the other races clocks.
When should I use Cross-Cutting?
Use it when two lines must tick together: raid and doorbell, vow and murder, two escapes. Do not use it as a pile of unused singles from one room.
How do I prompt Cross-Cutting for AI image or video?
Name both spaces and the race. Example: Cross-cutting between [Subject] and a simultaneous other line, two clocks racing. Keep the geographies distinct and the assumption of contact clear.
